original_title: CD Projekt says abandoning its in-house engine for The Witcher 4 had nothing to do with Cyberpunk 2077's technical woes: 'The dream of the company was actually never to make technology'

en.title: The Witcher 4 Ditches REDengine: CD Projekt Red Explains Why Now
en.summary: CD Projekt Red has officially confirmed The Witcher 4 will utilize Unreal Engine 5, moving away from their proprietary REDengine. Studio leadership clarifies this strategic shift is about future ambitions, not past technical struggles.
en.body:
The upcoming fourth installment in **The Witcher** saga is set to represent a monumental change for **CD Projekt Red**, not just in its narrative lead but also in its technological foundation. In a recent discussion, the studio’s co-CEO, **Michał Nowakowski**, clarified that the decision to abandon their long-standing REDengine in favor of **Unreal Engine 5** for **The Witcher 4** was a proactive, strategic choice, emphatically denying speculation that it was a direct response to the technical difficulties encountered during **Cyberpunk 2077**'s launch.

Nowakowski stressed that the issues surrounding **Cyberpunk 2077** were not inherent to the REDengine itself. Instead, he explained that the core motivation behind adopting **Unreal Engine 5** stems from a fundamental philosophy at **CD Projekt Red**. "The dream of the company was actually never to make technology," Nowakowski stated, highlighting that their primary focus has always been on crafting compelling narratives and immersive experiences. While the studio aimed to create "visually and technically cutting edge games," which led them to develop their own engine, the advent of **Unreal Engine 5** presented a new, more appealing path. Witnessing the capabilities of **Epic Games**' engine, particularly through demos like **The Matrix Awakens**, convinced leadership that a partnership with Epic would be more efficient than continuing to build and maintain their own complex technological infrastructure from scratch for each new project.

## A Strategic Leap, Not a Retreat

The shift to **Unreal Engine 5** is being framed as a strategic collaboration designed to accelerate development and leverage cutting-edge tools. Nowakowski elaborated that the REDengine required substantial rebuilding for each new title, a process that could be streamlined by adopting a robust third-party solution. "If we form a relationship with Unreal and if we work on certain things which are specifically required to make games of the size and scope and certain technicalities about it that we need for the games, it could actually work," he recalled thinking, leading to the "strategic collaboration" with Epic. This move allows **CD Projekt Red** to concentrate its resources on what it does best: storytelling and world-building, rather than diverting significant effort into engine development.

## Fan Reaction and Future Implications

For the passionate global fanbase of **The Witcher**, this announcement carries significant weight. While **Cyberpunk 2077**'s rocky launch left many concerned about the studio's technical prowess, this clarification should alleviate some of those worries. The move to **Unreal Engine 5** signals an intent to harness powerful, proven technology to deliver the high-quality, immersive experience fans expect from the franchise. The focus remains on delivering a game that pushes boundaries in narrative and gameplay, with the engine acting as a tool to achieve that vision. The community will undoubtedly be watching closely to see how this new technological foundation impacts the beloved world of Geralt and, now, Ciri.

## What's Next

While details on **The Witcher 4**'s development timeline and specific features remain under wraps, the commitment to **Unreal Engine 5** sets a clear direction. Fans can anticipate further updates from **CD Projekt Red** as development progresses on what is poised to be a landmark title for the studio and the franchise.

content_raw: We still don't know a huge amount about The Witcher 4 . But we do know it represents two big changes for the series thus far. The first change is, of course, that Ciri will replace Geralt as the lead character. The second is that CD Projekk will replace its in-house REDengine with Unreal Engine 5. There's been considerable speculation as to why CDP is abandoning tech that's delivered some of the most cutting-edge visuals of the last decade, with some fans suggesting that Cyberpunk 2077 's difficult development and compromised initial release might be a factor. But the studio's co-CEO Michał Nowakowski has formally dismissed this suggestion, stating the decision had more to do with CD Projekt's general ambitions than Cyberpunk specifically. Speaking on the Deconstructor of Fun podcast (via GamesRadar+ ), Nowakowski addressed the claim that Cyberpunk was the straw that broke REDengine's back: "A lot of people think like this, but this is a bit of a false assumption," he explained. "Because the issue with Cyberpunk was not really REDengine itself. Instead, Nowakowski said that CD Projekt never really wanted to be an engine developer in the first place, stating that. "The dream of the company was actually never to make technology." He conceded that CD Projekt did want to make "visually and technically cutting edge games", for which in-house tech seemed to be the optimal solution for the studio. But what ultimately drives the company is "telling the stories in the most convincing and immersive way." Hence, when CD Projekt's leadership saw The Matrix Awakens demo of Unreal Engine 5, they decided that adopting third-party tech would be preferable to continuing building their own tech. "If we form a relationship with Unreal and if we work on certain things which are specifically required to make games of the size and scope and certain technicalities about it that we need for games, it could actually work." With this in mind, CD Projekt pitched a "strategic collaboration" to Epic, where they would not simply license the tech but influence its direction from the inside. "We're actually, I think, the only team in the world outside of Epic that deals with the inside of the 'black box' that the engine is. Nobody else is doing that except for us and them, which we do through collaborative efforts together," Nowakowski remarked. It'll be interesting to see what impact CD Projekt's input has on Unreal Engine 5 going forward, since the tech has thus far gained a reputation for being a stuttering mess .
